column15: And this explains Deuteronomy 4:19: “which the Lord your God has apportioned unto all the peoples” — each nation drawing from a fragmented portion of supernal power. column11: Bereshit Rabbah 65:22: ‘“He did not recognize him, because his hands were hairy like the hands of his brother Esau, and he blessed him” (Genesis 27:23). “He did not recognize him” – when wicked people were produced from him, he [Isaac] did not recognize them. “His father Isaac said to him: Approach and kiss me, my son” (Genesis 27:26). “Approach and kiss me” – he said to him: ‘You will be adjacent to me in burial, but no other will be adjacent to me in burial.’ “He approached and kissed him, and he smelled the scent of his garments, and blessed him, and said: See, the scent of my son is as the scent of a field that the Lord blessed” (Genesis 27:27). “He approached and kissed him, and he smelled the scent of his…’ Context and connection to Likkutei Maamarim: In Likkutei Maamarim, Compositions on the Festivals 12, Rav Tzadok cites this midrashic exposition (Bereshit Rabbah 65:22) to illuminate his argument here (“as written in Bereishit Rabbah (65:22) on "as the smell of a field which Hashem has blessed" Genesis 27:27—this is an apple orchard; and this is "the scent of his traitors" (bogedav), even the missteps of Israel...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source grounds the spiritual dynamic of Torah, Israel's sanctity, and divine service developed in this discourse of Likkutei Maamarim.
column13: And there He is called “my beloved,” for nevertheless it came about through love and affection and not through suffering; but when it occurs through the afflictions of the nations, as they said regarding “a king as harsh as Haman” (Sanhedrin 97b), this is the awakening within the secret tunnel through the left hand that appears to reject, appearing cloaked in the hands that are “the hands of Esav.”, Just as the hands of Yaakov Avinu, peace be upon him, appeared when he came to receive the blessings from his father Yitzchak: for his hands were the very hands of Adam Elyon, since his form is engraved upon the Throne of Glory;],’ for the eye is ‘whitened’ [purified].”
column15: The meaning is that Isaac our Father grasped the attribute of Gevurah—darkness—manifesting in self-restraint toward all worldly matters out of transcendent awe before the Creator. Yet this very attribute itself requires measured restraint lest it expand excessively; for from an extreme distortion of this attribute branches the corrupt philosophical view adopted by wicked Esau.

column4: Likkutei Maamarim, Compositions on the Festivals 12
column11: Genesis 27:27: ‘and he went up and kissed him. And he smelled his clothes and he blessed him, saying, “Ah, the smell of my son is like the smell of the fields that GOD has blessed.’ Context and connection to Likkutei Maamarim: In Likkutei Maamarim, Compositions on the Festivals 12, Rav Tzadok cites this scriptural verse (Genesis 27:27) to illuminate his argument here (“as written in Bereishit Rabbah (65:22) on "as the smell of a field which Hashem has blessed" Genesis 27:27—this is an apple orchard; and this is "the scent of his traitors" (bogedav), even the missteps of Israel...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source grounds the spiritual dynamic of Torah, Israel's sanctity, and divine service developed in this discourse of Likkutei Maamarim.
column13: And 'even the empty ones among you are full of mitzvot like a pomegranate' (Sanhedrin 37a), and as written (there): 'He smelled the fragrance of his garments (begadav)—his betrayers (bogedav).' Nevertheless, there remain distinct spiritual gradations. Prayer essentially signifies connection and cleaving, and this explains why no man is spared from iyun tefillah: for in this, even Jacob's realm is not entirely uniform such that all would be identical and unified without levels in cleaving.
column15: And in Sifrei (Ha'azinu 309): A parable of one whose father bequeathed him ten fields, and he went and purchased one field of his own; that field he loved more than all the fields inherited from his father — meaning that because it was attained through his own labor, he feels deeper ownership than in what came gratis.

column4: Likkutei Maamarim, Compositions on the Festivals 12
column11: Sanhedrin 37a: ‘Reish Lakish says that the source to rely on them not to transgress is from here: “Your temples [rakkatekh] are like a pomegranate split open” (Song of Songs 6:7), which teaches that even the empty people [reikanin] among you are as full of mitzvot as the pomegranate is full of seeds. Rabbi Zeira says that the source is from here: The verse states concerning the occasion when Isaac blessed Jacob: “And he smelled the smell of his garments, and blessed him, and said: See, the smell of my son is as the smell of a field that the Lord has blessed” (Genesis 27:27). Do not read “his garments [begadav]”; rather, read: His traitors [bogedav], meaning that even traitors and sinners among the…’ Context and connection to Likkutei Maamarim: In Likkutei Maamarim, Compositions on the Festivals 12, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Sanhedrin 37a) to illuminate his argument here (“and this is "the scent of his traitors" (bogedav), even the missteps of Israel emitting a sweet fragrance; and this is the Sabbath sanctifying the six preceding workdays, retrospectively declaring that all was for...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source grounds the spiritual dynamic of Torah, Israel's sanctity, and divine service developed in this discourse of Likkutei Maamarim.
column13: Jacob's primary service, however, was anchored purely in sacred inward intention, his outer garments of deed emerging fully only with Laban—"With Laban I dwelled and the 613 commandments I kept"—where he began fathering the souls of Israel who embody the commandments. And woman embodies the dimension of action (Asiyah), which is why Rebecca clothed him in the garments of Esau; leading the Sages in Sanhedrin (37a) to expound "the smell of his garments (begadav)" as "the fragrance of his traitors (bogedav)".
column15: Yet in His lovingkindness Hashem credits the beginning to man, wherefore it says here: “And the Lord smelled the sweet savor; and the Lord said in His heart...” superficially implying that the awakening began below through the human resolve to constrict, stirring the oath on high.

column4: Likkutei Maamarim, Compositions on the Festivals 12
column11: Shabbat 88a: ‘Rabbi Elazar said: When the Jewish people accorded precedence to the declaration “We will do” over “We will hear,” a Divine Voice emerged and said to them: Who revealed to my children this secret that the ministering angels use? As it is written: “Bless the Lord, you angels of His, you mighty in strength, that fulfill His word, hearkening unto the voice of His word” (Psalms 103:20). At first, the angels fulfill His word, and then afterward they hearken. Rabbi Ḥama, son of Rabbi Ḥanina, said: What is the meaning of that which is written: “As an apple tree among the trees of the wood, so is my beloved among the sons. Under its shadow I delighted to sit and its fruit was sweet to my taste”…’ Context and connection to Likkutei Maamarim: In Likkutei Maamarim, Compositions on the Festivals 12, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Shabbat 88a) to illuminate his argument here (“And this is the apple tree, of which the Sages taught in Shabbat (88a): its fruit precedes its leaves, so Israel preceded "we will do" to "we will hear"; for the ultimate culmination of anything is its purpose, and...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source grounds the spiritual dynamic of Torah, Israel's sanctity, and divine service developed in this discourse of Likkutei Maamarim.
column13: Thus, fear is essential for words of Torah both at the beginning and at the end, and it constitutes the primary foundation, mirroring the inner rationale of 'we will do and we will hear,' fruit and its protective leaves (Shabbat 88a), and this is not the place to elaborate further.
column15: And it is stated in Midrash Rabbah (5:9) that the divine command was to bring forth a tree whose wood and fruit taste identical, yet the earth did not do so, producing merely a “tree bearing fruit” and not a “fruit-tree” whose bark itself is edible fruit.

column4: Likkutei Maamarim, Compositions on the Festivals 12
column11: Sukkah 21b: ‘The Gemara questions the formulation of the baraita. And let Rabbi Shimon say: From the statement of Rabban Gamliel. Why did he use the atypical expression: From the conversation of Rabban Gamliel? The Gemara answers: Through this expression he teaches us another matter in passing, like that which Rabbi Aḥa bar Adda said, and some say that Rabbi Aḥa bar Adda said that Rabbi Hamnuna said that Rav said: From where is it derived that even the conversation of Torah scholars require analysis, even when the intention of the speaker was apparently not to issue a halakhic ruling? It is as it is stated with regard to the righteous: “Which brings forth its fruit in its season and whose leaf does…’ Context and connection to Likkutei Maamarim: In Likkutei Maamarim, Compositions on the Festivals 12, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Sukkah 21b) to illuminate his argument here (“as written in Sukkah (21b) on "and his leaf does not wither" Psalms 1:3—even the casual conversation of scholars, and in Chullin (92a): the leaves and clusters represent the common folk and Torah scholars; yet there...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source grounds the spiritual dynamic of Torah, Israel's sanctity, and divine service developed in this discourse of Likkutei Maamarim.
column13: And so our Sages expounded (Sukkah 21b) on "and its leaf does not wither"—even the casual speech of scholars, which serves as the protective leaf for the cluster of Torah, and were it not for the leaf, the cluster could not endure, as written in Berakhot 35b: "Conduct yourself with them in the way of the world... I beg of you, etc., many did as Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai and did not succeed, because without the leaf, etc."
column15: As it is said: “And God said, Let the earth bring forth grass, herb yielding seed, and fruit tree”—which month is it when the earth puts forth grasses and trees are laden with fruit? You must say: this is Tishrei. Rabbi Yehoshua says: From where is it derived that the world was created in Nisan?

column4: Likkutei Maamarim, Compositions on the Festivals 12
column11: Psalms 1:3: ‘Such a one is like a tree planted beside streams of water,which yields its fruit in season,whose foliage never fades,and whatever it produces thrives.’ Context and connection to Likkutei Maamarim: In Likkutei Maamarim, Compositions on the Festivals 12, Rav Tzadok cites this scriptural verse (Psalms 1:3) to illuminate his argument here (“as written in Sukkah (21b) on "and his leaf does not wither" Psalms 1:3—even the casual conversation of scholars, and in Chullin (92a): the leaves and clusters represent the common folk and Torah scholars; yet there...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source grounds the spiritual dynamic of Torah, Israel's sanctity, and divine service developed in this discourse of Likkutei Maamarim.
column13: Regarding all the innate faculties planted within every soul of Israel, one must not imagine that any of them is pure evil requiring absolute eradication to its opposite; for you have no character trait or faculty that does not also possess a dimension of good, one only needs to utilize it in accordance with the will of the Blessed Name.
column15: And even if at times this realization cannot permeate everything, that is because man possesses personal ownership and grasp within it, and autonomous human activity is perishable like a withered bloom; and therefore a sown grain of wheat will not sprout until it entirely rots away and nothing remains save the central inner spark planted by the Blessed Name in the word “Bereishit”—that alone sprouts and yields fruit.

column4: Likkutei Maamarim, Compositions on the Festivals 12
column11: Chullin 92a: ‘Similar to Rabbi Yirmeya bar Abba’s interpretation of the word vine as an allusion to the Jewish people, Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish says: This nation is likened to a vine. The branches of the vine support the clusters of grapes, the leaves, and the tendrils; these are represented among the Jewish people by the homeowners, who provide financial support for the entire nation. The clusters of grapes on the vine, these are the Torah scholars. The leaves on the vine, which protect the grapes, these are the ignoramuses, who protect the Torah scholars. The tendrils of the vine, which do not directly serve the grapes themselves, these are the empty ones of the Jewish people.’ Context and connection to Likkutei Maamarim: In Likkutei Maamarim, Compositions on the Festivals 12, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Chullin 92a) to illuminate his argument here (“and in Chullin (92a): the leaves and clusters represent the common folk and Torah scholars; yet there it states: were it not for the leaves the clusters could not endure, the foliage sheltering the vine. And looking...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source grounds the spiritual dynamic of Torah, Israel's sanctity, and divine service developed in this discourse of Likkutei Maamarim.
column13: And even this—is only for the moment, and it is not yet entirely slain, but immediately afterward returns to its place, requiring renewed toil to conquer it every day and every hour. Only that with respect to Jacob this was a trivial, effortless matter, and in the phrasing of our Sages there, 12: like one removing the cork from the mouth of a flask.
column15: As we have seen that Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai, his entire holy labor was focused on the word “Bereishit,” refining and recombining the word “Bereishit” in seventy ways throughout the Holy Zohar and the Tikkunim. And that is: so that the souls of Israel may be clarified as having no guile in their spirit, and that the fundamental root of Israel is pure of all dross and waste.

column4: Likkutei Maamarim, Compositions on the Festivals 12
column11: Pirkei Avot 3:9: ‘Rabbi Hanina ben Dosa said: anyone whose fear of sin precedes his wisdom, his wisdom is enduring, but anyone whose wisdom precedes his fear of sin, his wisdom is not enduring. He [also] used to say: anyone whose deeds exceed his wisdom, his wisdom is enduring, but anyone whose wisdom exceeds his deeds, his wisdom is not enduring.’ Context and connection to Likkutei Maamarim: In Likkutei Maamarim, Compositions on the Festivals 12, Rav Tzadok cites this midrashic exposition (Pirkei Avot 3:9) to illuminate his argument here (“and within man himself: performing deeds sustains his wisdom (Avot 3:9), wisdom being the true fruit. And this holds looking forward from the vantage of moral free will, conquering the inclination being possible only...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source grounds the spiritual dynamic of Torah, Israel's sanctity, and divine service developed in this discourse of Likkutei Maamarim.
column13: Fear is the attribute of Knesset Yisrael as is known, meaning that all Israel possess fear of Heaven, even the common folk. Only a boor lacks fear of sin, because he lacks derekh eretz, whereas the derekh eretz of Israel is itself fear of Heaven. And therefore derekh eretz precedes the Torah, as written: whoever's fear precedes his wisdom, his wisdom endures (Avot 3:9).
column15: And as taught in Avot (3:14): “Beloved is man that he was created in the image of God; an especially great love was made known to him in that he was created in the image” — for man's essential acquisition is suspended upon conscious knowledge.

column4: Likkutei Maamarim, Compositions on the Festivals 12
column11: Kiddushin 30b: ‘A Sage from the school of Rabbi Yishmael taught: My son, if this wretched one, the evil inclination, encounters you, pull it into the study hall, i.e., go and study Torah. If it is a stone it will melt, and if it is iron it will break, as it is stated with regard to the Torah: “Is not My word like fire, says the Lord, and like a hammer that breaks the rock in pieces?” (Jeremiah 23:29). Just as a stone shatters a hammer, so too one can overcome his evil inclination, which is as strong as iron, through Torah study. With regard to the second part of the statement: If it is a stone it will melt, this is as it is stated with regard to the Torah: “Ho, everyone who thirsts, come for water”…’ Context and connection to Likkutei Maamarim: In Likkutei Maamarim, Compositions on the Festivals 12, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Kiddushin 30b) to illuminate his argument here (“conquering the inclination being possible only through wisdom: "I created the Torah as a condiment" (Kiddushin 30b); the purpose of free will being that man deliberately choose good over evil: "therefore choose life"...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source grounds the spiritual dynamic of Torah, Israel's sanctity, and divine service developed in this discourse of Likkutei Maamarim.
column13: The rectification for emitting seed in vain is engagement in Torah study, as written (Kiddushin 30b): "I created the evil inclination, I created the Torah as its antidote"; and they stated in Sukkah 52a: the Holy One, blessed be He, called it "evil," which refers to the sin of the Generation of the Flood, namely emitting seed in vain and they said in Kiddushin 13a that the decree did not fall upon the fish of the sea, which represent Torah scholars, as I wrote elsewhere on "and have dominion over the fish of the sea".
column15: This constitutes no moral virtue, being imprisoned within instinct, unable to depart from their fixed nature; whereas man through free choice can deliberate, turning himself from one attribute to its opposite. Hence man can live in no element except Air, Air matching his soul-root, perishing if submerged in Earth, Water, or Fire.

column4: Likkutei Maamarim, Compositions on the Festivals 12
column11: Deuteronomy 30:19: ‘I call heaven and earth to witness against you this day: I have put before you life and death, blessing and curse. Choose life—if you and your offspring would live—’ Context and connection to Likkutei Maamarim: In Likkutei Maamarim, Compositions on the Festivals 12, Rav Tzadok cites this scriptural verse (Deuteronomy 30:19) to illuminate his argument here (“the purpose of free will being that man deliberately choose good over evil: "therefore choose life" Deuteronomy 30:19; so that prospective striving centers in wisdom wherein resides choice, making it the fruit,...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source grounds the spiritual dynamic of Torah, Israel's sanctity, and divine service developed in this discourse of Likkutei Maamarim.
column13: And although prior to the Fall Adam recognized that the Blessed Name is the supreme Ruler; nevertheless, through the very fact that the Holy One was compelled to warn him—which represents the faculty of free will that the Blessed Name desired in His universe—; through which human striving and the ultimate purpose of Creation are achieved: "See, I have set before you... life and death... therefore choose life" (Devarim 30:19–20); through this the Serpent misled him, making it appear as though the Blessed Name did not govern all things completely and directly from Heaven.
column15: Proving that all human acquisition is defined by conscious knowledge. Wherefore this was the purpose of concealment in this world—generating the reality of free choice and labor—so that man might secure eternal reward when Hashem opens His light, still tasting the sweet fulfillment of earned toil.

column4: Likkutei Maamarim, Compositions on the Festivals 12
column11: Shabbat 49a: ‘Come and hear a resolution to this dilemma from the materials listed in the mishna: And one may neither insulate a pot in straw, nor in the residue of grapes that have been pressed for their juice, nor in soft materials, nor in grass, when these materials are moist. Granted, if you say that the mishna is referring to materials that are moist due to something else, this can be well understood, as all of these materials can get wet. However, if you say that it is referring to materials that are moist due to their own natural state, where do you find soft materials that are moist due to their own natural state? Wool is dry in its natural state. The Gemara rejects this argument: The mishna…’ Context and connection to Likkutei Maamarim: In Likkutei Maamarim, Compositions on the Festivals 12, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Shabbat 49a) to illuminate his argument here (“for deed remains the bedrock, mitzvot acting as a shield (Shabbat 49a), protecting lest one stumble in speculation without practical observance. Yet the Sages concluded in Berakhot (17a): The ultimate purpose of...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source grounds the spiritual dynamic of Torah, Israel's sanctity, and divine service developed in this discourse of Likkutei Maamarim.
column13: And as for why they did not define this likewise for Israel, the Asarah Ma'amaros was hard-pressed to explain [ibid.], suggesting that committing sexual sin out of disdain for the prohibition does not occur in Israel but only among gentiles, see there; yet there is no substance to this, and in my opinion it is simple: a sin involving physical lust is presumed to be driven by appetite (l'tei'avon), just as I wrote regarding circumcision; and in an Israelite such a case is not categorized as "sinners of Israel with their bodies" unless performed by way of defiance and contempt.
column15: And as taught (Niddah 61b): “Mitzvot are abolished in the World to Come”; and they are forbidden now only because it is before their time—had Adam waited, he would have been permitted to eat. For the essence of prohibition is that it dulls the heart and binds the intellect, preventing man from returning to Hashem as before eating; whereas had he waited, Hashem would have granted him expanded consciousness to receive it without forgetting the Creator.

column4: Likkutei Maamarim, Compositions on the Festivals 12
column11: Berakhot 17a: ‘Rava was wont to say: The objective of Torah wisdom is to achieve repentance and good deeds; that one should not read the Torah and study mishna and become arrogant and spurn his father and his mother and his teacher and one who is greater than he in wisdom or in the number of students who study before him, as it is stated: “The beginning of wisdom is fear of the Lord, a good understanding have all who fulfill them” (Psalms 111:10). It is not stated simply: All who fulfill, but rather: All who fulfill them, those who perform these actions as they ought to be performed, meaning those who do such deeds for their own sake, for the sake of the deeds themselves, not those who do them not for…’ Context and connection to Likkutei Maamarim: In Likkutei Maamarim, Compositions on the Festivals 12, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Berakhot 17a) to illuminate his argument here (“Yet the Sages concluded in Berakhot (17a): The ultimate purpose of wisdom is repentance and good deeds; this being the overarching goal in this world: actualizing the divine will in physical deed, wherefore the...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source grounds the spiritual dynamic of Torah, Israel's sanctity, and divine service developed in this discourse of Likkutei Maamarim.
column13: But in my opinion, were it not for the words of Tosafos in Bava Metzia, it would have seemed plain to me: that what they stated in Eruvin there, "that refers to those who are liable for that hour"; did not mean a literal measure of one hour out of the twenty-four hours of the day, for what rationale is there for such a duration? And furthermore, the phrasing "who are liable" implies that they are not liable in judgment for any further punishment for their iniquity.
column15: And the meaning of attending unto the Blessed Name is that one should gaze upon the inner root of all the deeds performed throughout the six workdays, contemplating how they appear before the Blessed Name, and what spiritual countenance his mundane deeds and outer garments reflect relative to the divine Will which is the origin of all actions.

column4: Likkutei Maamarim, Compositions on the Festivals 12
column11: Menachot 29b: ‘Rav Ashi responded: It is as Rabbi Yehuda bar Rabbi Elai taught: The verse “For in the Lord [beYah] is God, an everlasting Rock [Tzur olamim]” is understood as follows: The term “Tzur olamim” can also mean Creator of worlds. These letters yod and heh that constitute the word yah are referring to the two worlds that the Holy One, Blessed be He, created; one with [be] the letter heh and one with [be] the letter yod. And I do not know whether the World-to-Come was created with the letter yod and this world was created with the letter heh, or whether this world was created with the letter yod and the World-to-Come was created with the letter heh.’ Context and connection to Likkutei Maamarim: In Likkutei Maamarim, Compositions on the Festivals 12, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Menachot 29b) to illuminate his argument here (“as written in Menachot (29b): this world created with Heh (action) and the World to Come with Yud (thought), the letter Heh signifying deed in the Zohar, this being the core of this world: "this day to do them, and...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source grounds the spiritual dynamic of Torah, Israel's sanctity, and divine service developed in this discourse of Likkutei Maamarim.
column13: Therefore, even though Moses our Teacher did not understand the advanced deductions of Rabbi Akiva in Menachot (29b), his mind was set at ease when a student asked Rabbi Akiva: "From where do you know this? Lest you have erred?", and he answered: "It is a Halachah given to Moses at Sinai"—for with Moses our Teacher there is no possibility of error.
column15: And in Zohar Mikeitz (200a): “Thought is the inception of all, and word is the culmination of all.” For as long as a concept remains within contemplation, will, and thought, no external person can perceive it; and even when manifested in action, the inward thought is not definitively clear, as he can still explain his intent differently from how another interprets it.

column4: Likkutei Maamarim, Compositions on the Festivals 12
column11: Eruvin 22a: ‘And that is what Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi said: What is the meaning of that which is written: “And you shall keep the commandments, and the statutes, and the judgments which I command you today to do them” (Deuteronomy 7:11)? It means: Today is the time to do them, in this world, and tomorrow is not the time to do them, as there is no obligation or opportunity to fulfill mitzvot in the World-to-Come. Furthermore, it means: Today is the time to do them, but only tomorrow, in the ultimate future, is the time to receive reward for doing them.’ Context and connection to Likkutei Maamarim: In Likkutei Maamarim, Compositions on the Festivals 12, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Eruvin 22a) to illuminate his argument here (“this being the core of this world: "this day to do them, and tomorrow to receive their reward" Eruvin 22a; the reward being the wisdom and perception of Hashem's truth in the World to Come. Wherefore in this world...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source grounds the spiritual dynamic of Torah, Israel's sanctity, and divine service developed in this discourse of Likkutei Maamarim.
column13: Meaning that all is one: enduring permanence occurs only when the halachah follows him, which would have established Saul's kingdom forever. And the literal meaning of yarshi'a in the biblical text refers to his military campaigns against the nations, where he triumphed over them and convicted them. And certainly a verse does not lose its plain meaning, as regarding David being described as "a mighty man of valor and a man of war", for all their battles were waged strictly by Hashem's command and divine success, and not through mere natural physical valor.
column15: And this occurs as the Name Adonai serves as the outer sheath for Havayah in this world, requiring man to endure toil and patience. Even though human self-restraint is on a lowly plane and of minute scale, as written: “this day upon your heart,” expounded in Mei HaShiloach regarding the Men of Jericho (Pesachim 56a): today the mitzvot rest externally “upon your heart,” while in the World to Come they will be ingrained internally “within your heart.”

column4: Likkutei Maamarim, Compositions on the Festivals 12
column11: Isaiah 60:21: ‘And your people, all of them righteous,Shall possess the land for all time;They are the shoot that I planted,My handiwork in which I glory.’ Context and connection to Likkutei Maamarim: In Likkutei Maamarim, Compositions on the Festivals 12, Rav Tzadok cites this scriptural verse (Isaiah 60:21) to illuminate his argument here (“And "Your people are all righteous" Isaiah 60:21 in deed, "they shall inherit the land forever" because in eternity they will attain wisdom as well. And though free will requires less fierce struggle for them—since...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source grounds the spiritual dynamic of Torah, Israel's sanctity, and divine service developed in this discourse of Likkutei Maamarim.
column13: And [Korach and his assembly] came to dispute his authority with the argument: "all the congregation are holy... wherefore then lift ye up yourselves?" (Bamidbar 16:3); meaning that a Torah scholar has no superiority over an am ha'aretz, for "Your people are all righteous" and inherit the earth and the World to Come; for even the empty ones of Israel are as full of mitzvos as a pomegranate as they said [in Berachos 57a], which refers to an am ha'aretz who is empty of Torah knowledge.
column15: And this is: “Your people also shall be all righteous”—that within the people of Israel resides the power of constriction, which is the unifying foundation harmonizing all attributes in equal balance, so that no single trait displaces its fellow.

column4: Likkutei Maamarim, Compositions on the Festivals 12
column11: Sukkah 52a: ‘It is stated: “The land will eulogize, each family separately; the family of the house of David separately, and their women separately, the family of the house of Nathan separately, and their women separately” (Zechariah 12:12). This indicates that at the end of days a great eulogy will be organized during which men and women will be separate. They said: And are these matters not inferred a fortiori? If in the future, at the end of days referred to in this prophecy, when people are involved in a great eulogy and consequently the evil inclination does not dominate them, as typically during mourning inappropriate thoughts and conduct are less likely, and nevertheless the Torah says: Men…’ Context and connection to Likkutei Maamarim: In Likkutei Maamarim, Compositions on the Festivals 12, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Sukkah 52a) to illuminate his argument here (“And though free will requires less fierce struggle for them—since "whoever is greater than his fellow, his inclination is greater" (Sukkah 52a)— moral struggle intensifying in proportion to wisdom; and prospectively,...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source grounds the spiritual dynamic of Torah, Israel's sanctity, and divine service developed in this discourse of Likkutei Maamarim.
column13: As it is known of "one corresponding to the other": wherever a greater root of holiness exists, the opposing evil is correspondingly potent, in the manner stated (Sukkah 52a): "Whoever is greater than his fellow has a greater inclination than him"; and within Esau resided an immense root of holiness from two Patriarchs, closely approaching the sanctity of Jacob our father, for "was not Esau brother to Jacob?", and until they matured their differing natures were not outwardly distinguishable, as our Sages taught (Bereishit Rabbah ibid.).
column15: This is why these conquering nations are mentioned in the verse: “The Caphtorim who came out of Caphtor destroyed them, etc.” For although the Caphtorim possessed less raw physical power, because they had greater free will to govern their bodies, they conquered the earlier inhabitants; since one endowed with moral choice can overcome one who lacks choice.

column11: Shabbat 88a: ‘Rabbi Simai taught: When Israel accorded precedence to the declaration “We will do” over the declaration “We will hear,” 600,000 ministering angels came and tied two crowns to each and every member of the Jewish people, one corresponding to “We will do” and one corresponding to “We will hear.” And when the people sinned with the Golden Calf, 1,200,000 angels of destruction descended and removed them from the people, as it is stated in the wake of the sin of the Golden Calf: “And the children of Israel stripped themselves of their ornaments from Mount Horeb onward” (Exodus 33:6). Rabbi Ḥama, son of Rabbi Ḥanina, said: At Horeb they put on their ornaments, and at Horeb they removed them.…’ Context and connection to Likkutei Maamarim: In Likkutei Maamarim, Compositions on the Festivals 12, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Shabbat 88a) to illuminate his argument here (“And this is what the Sages stated in Shabbat (88a): that preceding "we will do" to "we will hear" is the mystery utilized by the ministering angels; for this reflects the transcendence of free will: for from the...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source grounds the spiritual dynamic of Torah, Israel's sanctity, and divine service developed in this discourse of Likkutei Maamarim.
column12: Sichat Malakhei HaSharet, A Note on Angels' Names:6 (§4)
column13: And the Sages taught in Shabbat (88a) regarding the crowns bestowed upon Israel at Mount Sinai: that this was measure for measure: through their twin declarations of "we will do" and "we will hear" they crowned their Maker, and measure for measure the Blessed Name crowned them as well. For the essence of a crown is that which regarding King David is called the "testimony" (edut), the crown fitting him precisely (Avodah Zarah 44a), a monarch possessing a royal crown crowning him with this glory.
column15: And this stemmed from the fact that he saw explicitly that he was the handiwork of the Holy One, both in soul and in body; and the radiance of his physical heel outshone the ministering angels (Likutei Torah of the Ari; Zohar Kedoshim 83b); if so, how could such a sublime body possibly possess the impulse to turn away from the divine Will?

column13: Therefore they said [in Avos d’Rabbi Nasan] that “all their conversation is [inclined to] immorality” — so that, “as water [reflects] face to face,” “her voice arouses love and desire in the heart of the man.” And likewise, “Israel’s longing is only for the Holy One,” and therefore “their voice arouses His love for them” — and then “the love is revealed,” so that “man too no longer considers himself hated.” — the cry itself is what elicits the love: as a face answers a face in water, Israel’s yearning voice draws forth the very love whose absence it had mourned.
column15: And seemingly it is astonishing: Why did the earth not fulfill the explicit command of the Blessed Name? The explanation of this is: over the wood of the tree itself rests the Name Ehyeh , which signifies that which is poised within the divine Will to bestow but has not yet actualized into tangible reality; as in the Zohar (Acharei Mot 65b) that this Name means: “I am prepared to bring forth birth”.

Rabbi Levi said: Were Israel to repent even…’ Context and connection to Likkutei Maamarim: In Likkutei Maamarim, Compositions on the Festivals 12, Rav Tzadok cites this midrashic exposition (Shir HaShirim Rabbah 5:2) to illuminate his argument here (“Yet through absolute unity, "I am Hashem Who dwells in the midst of Israel," God being the true heart of Israel (Shir HaShirim Rabbah 5:2), being entirely unsevered from Him, they are likewise called by the Name of...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source grounds the spiritual dynamic of Torah, Israel's sanctity, and divine service developed in this discourse of Likkutei Maamarim.
column13: The moment a person desires to repent, behold he is "coming to purify himself," and the heavenly rule is to assist him, as written in Yoma 38b; and when they assist him, there is automatically added within him a spirit of purity, prompting him to strive further to purify himself; and then assistance from Above returns with even greater intensity, leading him below to strive further to purify himself; and so it cycles repeatedly, until from an opening as narrow as the eye of a needle it expands into the portal of the Temple Hall (Shir HaShirim Rabbah 5:2).
column15: Thus Noah was saved from the Flood, but had to flee into the Ark; for one who is completely pure and righteous needs no ark, deliverance standing abundant before Hashem, just as Moses and all who went out of Egypt walked in the midst of the sea on dry ground, requiring no ark.

column11: Eruvin 19a: ‘If the golden altar in the Temple, which was only covered by gold the thickness of a golden dinar, stood for many years and the fire did not burn it, for its gold did not melt, so too the sinners of the Jewish people, who are filled with good deeds like a pomegranate, as it is stated: “Your temples [rakatekh] are like a split pomegranate behind your veil” (Song of Songs 6:7), will not be affected by the fire of Gehenna. And Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish said about this: Do not read: Your temples [rakatekh], but rather: Your empty ones [reikateikh], meaning that even the sinners among you are full of mitzvot like a pomegranate; how much more so should the fire of Gehenna have no power over them.’ Context and connection to Likkutei Maamarim: In Likkutei Maamarim, Compositions on the Festivals 12, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Eruvin 19a) to illuminate his argument here (“And this is "the scent of his traitors": even the sinners of Israel are filled with mitzvot like a pomegranate (Eruvin 19a), and though their conscious choice erred toward evil, beyond all choice their core soul...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source grounds the spiritual dynamic of Torah, Israel's sanctity, and divine service developed in this discourse of Likkutei Maamarim.
column13: For the dross of fire is the fire of Gehinnom wherein the wicked are judged; while the hot springs of Tiberias pass over the entrance of Gehinnom for Israel to luxuriate in them (Eruvin 19a); wherefore "Rakkath is Tiberias—for even the empty (reikanin) within it are full of mitzvos like a pomegranate" (Megillah 6a); wherefore the subterranean fire of Gehinnom destined for the empty is transformed for them into soothing hot water to cleanse the body; and to luxuriate in honor of Shabbat by washing in hot water (Shabbat 25b).
column15: This is explained as taught in Tikkunei Zohar (Tikkun 14, 30a) regarding meat and milk mirroring “You shall not plow with an ox and an ass together”: Rabbi Shimon said: An ox is pure and an ass is impure, forming mixed species of good and evil; but milk is pure and meat is pure!

column11: Shabbat 89b: ‘MISHNA: After an extended digression for a discussion of matters unrelated to the halakhot of Shabbat, this mishna resumes treatment of the halakhot of carrying from domain to domain on Shabbat. One who carries out wood on Shabbat is liable for a measure equivalent to the amount of wood necessary to cook an easily cooked egg. The measure that determines liability for carrying out spices is equivalent to that which is used to season an easily cooked egg. And all types of spices join together with one another to constitute the measure for liability. The measure that determines liability for carrying out nutshells, pomegranate peels, safflower, and madder, which are used to produce dyes, is…’ Context and connection to Likkutei Maamarim: In Likkutei Maamarim, Compositions on the Festivals 12, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Shabbat 89b) to illuminate his argument here (“automatically their missteps were preordained from the Six Days of Creation (Shabbat 89b), utilized by the divine plan. column13: And David HaMelech is the rectifier of the inclination of licentiousness — through his “sin” being clarified: that Scripture too reckons upon him a “complete sin,” and that “[he did] evil in the eyes of Hashem,” yet he was truly “full of holiness,” for she was fit for him from the six days of Creation; and so all the sins of the Children of Israel are “arranged and come from the six days of Creation,” and then “they shall become white as snow”; and the one who completes [it] will be Mashiach ben David, in whose days the inclination will be wholly swallowed up.

column11: Shabbat 77b: ‘A barrel is called kufta, which is an acronym for kuf vetiv, which means turn it over and sit. Bricks are called livnei, which is an allusion to livnei benei, which means for the children of children. A fence made of thorns is called hutza and Rav Yehuda said that it is merely a ḥatzitza, which means partition, as opposed to a true fence. A jug used for drawing water is called a ḥatzba because it hews [ḥotzev] water from the river. A small jug is called kuza, alluding to kazeh, which means: Give me one like that. Myrtle branches with which people dance at a wedding are called shutita, an allusion to shetuta, which means madness, as the frenzied dancing appears to be madness. The large…’ Context and connection to Likkutei Maamarim: In Likkutei Maamarim, Compositions on the Festivals 12, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Shabbat 77b) to illuminate his argument here (“And in the creation of the cosmos, first was darkness and then light, evening preceding; while in the creation of man the reverse occurred: the male was formed first, followed by the female; mirroring the Sabbath day...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source grounds the spiritual dynamic of Torah, Israel's sanctity, and divine service developed in this discourse of Likkutei Maamarim.

column13: In Berakhot (2a): "The Tanna derives the precedence of the evening Shema from the Creation of the world ['and there was evening and there was morning, one day']," etc., see there: for in sacrificial offerings (Kodashim), night follows day, where the light of morning precedes the evening darkness; even though in the physical Creation of the cosmos, darkness came first and light followed (Shabbat 77b).
column15: And their entire desire was merely to establish an enduring foundation for the existence of the cosmos, that it never collapse again. Therefore they called the Name of the Holy One upon idols, for their sole ambition was to flee from before their Master, so that the divine light would be concealed in this world through the sheath and dividing partition they erected through their actions, diminishing the overt light of Hashem in this world, whereby they mistakenly believed the world's endurance would be fortified.

column11: Shabbat 69b: ‘Rav Huna said: One who was walking along the way or in the desert, and he does not know when Shabbat occurs, he counts six days from the day that he realized that he lost track of Shabbat and then observes one day as Shabbat. Ḥiyya bar Rav says: He first observes one day as Shabbat and then he counts six weekdays. The Gemara explains: With regard to what do they disagree? One Sage, Rav Huna, held: It is like the creation of the world, weekdays followed by Shabbat. And one Sage, Ḥiyya bar Rav, held: It is like Adam, the first man, who was created on the sixth day. He observed Shabbat followed by the six days of the week. The Gemara raises an objection to the opinion of Ḥiyya bar Rav from…’ Context and connection to Likkutei Maamarim: In Likkutei Maamarim, Compositions on the Festivals 12, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Shabbat 69b) to illuminate his argument here (“while Adam counted in reverse, sanctifying the Sabbath first Shabbat 69b; for man operating in free will must place the Sabbath first—"What is Shabbat? The Name of the Holy One"— acquiring clear perception that "He...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source grounds the spiritual dynamic of Torah, Israel's sanctity, and divine service developed in this discourse of Likkutei Maamarim.
column13: Where the hybrid is also integrated into Creation, for then is the realm of divine service without the evil inclination, which is the service of “with all your heart—with both inclinations”, and then is completed “and behold it was very good” stated at the end of the sixth day, which our Sages expounded: this is the evil inclination; and this occurs at the twilight of the sixth millennium, which is immediately adjacent to Shabbat, the World to Come; where even the raw inclination is harnessed into holy Creation.
column15: Because Adam HaRishon perceived clearly that his sin had been set up along the lines of “He is awesome in His deeds toward the children of men” (Psalms 66:5), as in Tanchuma (Vayeishev 4): “The awesome decrees You bring upon us, You bring through pretext; come and see: when the Holy One created the world, from the very first day He created the Angel of Death, etc.”

column11: Zohar, Yitro 27:453-464: ‘In this time of satisfaction and goodwill Moses, the holy, faithful prophet, passed away from this world, in order that it should be known that he was not taken away through judgement,but that in the hour of grace of the Holy Ancient One his soul ascended, to be hidden in Him. Therefore “no man knows of his sepulchre unto this day” (Deut. 34, 6). As the Holy Ancient One is the All-hidden One, whom neither those above nor those below can comprehend, so was this soul of Moses hidden in the epiphany of God’s good will at the hour of the Sabbath afternoon prayer. This soul is the most hidden of all hidden things in the world, and judgement has no dominion over it. Blessed is the lot of Moses.’ Context and connection to Likkutei Maamarim: In Likkutei Maamarim, Compositions on the Festivals 12, Rav Tzadok cites this kabbalistic teaching (Zohar, Yitro 27:453-464) to illuminate his argument here (“for man operating in free will must place the Sabbath first—"What is Shabbat? The Name of the Holy One"— acquiring clear perception that "He gives you power to get wealth" Deuteronomy 8:18; and only after this...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source grounds the spiritual dynamic of Torah, Israel's sanctity, and divine service developed in this discourse of Likkutei Maamarim.
column13: And the three mitzvot were given to rectify the blemish in nefesh, ruach, and neshamah. Therefore the mitzvot of challah and niddah apply every day, while candle lighting is uniquely on Shabbat, based on what is written in the holy Zohar in this parashah (62a): nefesh and ruach are intertwined with one another, etc.; when a man comes to purify himself— they assist him with a holy neshamah, etc., and sanctify him, and he is called holy.
column15: As my revered father, the holy Gaon of Izbica, of blessed memory, explained: this is why the Men of the Great Assembly arranged the Shabbat Musaf prayer with backward alphabetical order (Tashrak), because this indicates that on Shabbat the letters face inward toward the Emanator, appearing reversed before human mortal eyes; meaning that on the Sabbath a person must aspire to will only that which is the pure will of the Blessed Name, setting aside his personal agendas and setting up no independent receptacle of his own.

column11: Deuteronomy 8:18: ‘Remember that it is the ETERNAL your God who gives you the power to get wealth, in fulfillment of the covenant made on oath with your fathers, as is still the case.’ Context and connection to Likkutei Maamarim: In Likkutei Maamarim, Compositions on the Festivals 12, Rav Tzadok cites this scriptural verse (Deuteronomy 8:18) to illuminate his argument here (“acquiring clear perception that "He gives you power to get wealth" Deuteronomy 8:18; and only after this awareness should he go forth to engage his active labors. And this is the third meal corresponding to Ze'eir...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source grounds the spiritual dynamic of Torah, Israel's sanctity, and divine service developed in this discourse of Likkutei Maamarim.
column13: Which is not so with the Children of Israel, where the sufferings are only “as a father chastens his son” (Devarim 8:5)” — “and you shall know in your heart, that just as a man chastens his son, so Hashem your God chastens you.” Background: Moshe frames the wilderness trials as a father’s loving discipline, not punishment. Meforshim: these are yissurin shel ahavah — “sufferings of love” (cf. Berachos 5a). R’ Tzadok’s use: here is the whole distinction between the nations and Israel — over the nations Malchus pours out lethal wrath, but Israel’s sufferings “are only as a father chastening his son, to give him life and to better his end thereby.”

column15: Different is Israel, Hashem's portion and His people, to whom Hashem channels bounty progressively with an abundant, generous eye, and they possess the realization that Hashem is the One Who gives them power to get wealth, having no independent claim on their own part in Hashem's influx; therefore they too possess a true partnership in the influx.

column11: Sanhedrin 97b: ‘The Gemara asks: And are those who view the Divine Presence through a crystal that is luminous so numerous? If they number one thousand, I and my son are among them. If they number one hundred, I and my son are among them; and if they number two, I and my son are they. column13: And healing is for the illness in the soul itself, to be saved from the “leaven in the dough” itself; and redemption is from the enslavement to kingdoms; and this is the rung of Moshe Rabbeinu, who is the first redeemer of Israel. And at the time of matan Torah, when the past was rectified, there came to be complete freedom from the kingdoms, from the yetzer hara, and even from the Angel of Death, as it will be in the future. — meaning the zuhama that the serpent injected [into Chavah], which is desire [ta’avah], in the language of the Sages.”
column15: As taught in the Zohar (Mishpatim 114a): “‘And the writing was the writing of God’—black fire upon white fire.” “The writing of God was it (hu)”—alluding to (Numbers 18:23): “and the Levite shall serve, he (hu)” (see below, section 17).

column11: Megillah 6b: ‘The Gemara comments: This applies only to matters of Torah, as success with respect to Torah study is in accordance with the toil and effort invested. But with regard to success in business, it all depends upon assistance from Heaven, as there is no correlation between success and effort. And even with regard to matters of Torah, we said this only with regard to sharpening one’s understanding of Torah, as the more one labors, the deeper the understanding of the material he achieves. However, to preserve what one has learned, it is dependent upon assistance from Heaven. Not everyone achieves this, even with much effort.’ Context and connection to Likkutei Maamarim: In Likkutei Maamarim, Compositions on the Festivals 12, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Megillah 6b) to illuminate his argument here (“and regarding Torah it is said: "if you toiled and found, believe it" (Megillah 6b), "It is not in heaven," but given to Israel according to their toil. And the Boethusians/Sadducees who insisted that Shavuot must...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source grounds the spiritual dynamic of Torah, Israel's sanctity, and divine service developed in this discourse of Likkutei Maamarim.
column13: A faith indestructible across time, which Habakkuk established upon a single foundation: "And the righteous shall live by his faith" (Makkot 24a), for while individual commandments may be restricted by circumstance, faith can never be nullified; providing supreme guidance for anyone seeking deliverance from personal darkness: fortifying oneself in faith that Hashem is with him everywhere, dissolving harm because Hashem is his light; shining brighter until the full day arrives, which is why we link the redemption of Adar to the redemption of Nisan (Megillah 6b).
column15: Had it stemmed from Eve alone, no sin would have existed at all—and all the more so in the future when the sin is rectified, an immense light will radiate from this. And once Adam HaRishon comprehended that through her he attained this exalted level—for on his own he would never have entered moral doubt, she alone having drawn him into it— he recognized that not merely as a helper was she given to him, but that she elevates him in the ways of Hashem regarding realms transcending his intellect, true life flowing to him through her.

column11: Menachot 65a: ‘The Gemara discusses the next period listed in the baraita: From the eighth of Nisan until the end of the festival of Passover, the correct date for the festival of Shavuot was restored, and it was similarly decreed not to eulogize during this period. As the Boethusians would say that the festival of Shavuot always occurs after Shabbat, on a Sunday. Their reasoning was that the verse states, with regard to the omer offering and the festival of Shavuot that follows seven weeks later: “And you shall count for you from the morrow after the day of rest [hashabbat], from the day that you brought the sheaf [omer] of the waving; seven weeks shall there be complete” (Leviticus 23:15).…’ Context and connection to Likkutei Maamarim: In Likkutei Maamarim, Compositions on the Festivals 12, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Menachot 65a) to illuminate his argument here (“And the Boethusians/Sadducees who insisted that Shavuot must fall on a Sunday following the Sabbath—celebrated as a festival in Megillat Ta'anit when their view was refuted (Menachot 65a)— the root of their heresy...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source grounds the spiritual dynamic of Torah, Israel's sanctity, and divine service developed in this discourse of Likkutei Maamarim.

column13: In the Amidah prayer this supplication is articulated in individual detail, whereas in Ashrei it is declared collectively; therefore Ashrei is required three times daily parallel to the three daily prayers, for three repetitions establish an enduring reality (chazakah), and such is the standard calibration of the Sages, as in the reaping of the Omer (Menachot 65a) and other rituals where threefold verbal affirmation is required.
column15: And for this reason the Blessed Name positioned the Sabbath day following the six workdays: to instruct that after man has broadly indulged his energies across permissible secular pursuits during the weekdays, his mind becoming agitated and distracted, upon the arrival of the Seventh Day he must draw back, constricting his active drives so as to return all vitality to the Blessed Name.

column11: Kiddushin 66a: ‘And had Abaye taught us only the case of: Your ritually pure food was rendered ritually impure, one might have said that the reason this witness is deemed credible is that he causes him a loss on his days of ritual purity, and therefore his silence is tantamount to a confession. column13: And the tragedy of the Temple's destruction is likewise placed in Gittin in the chapter HaNizakin; wherefore the tractate concludes: one who divorces his first wife causes the Altar to shed tears, because from their viewpoint it is clarified that divorce is permissible only for marital infidelity according to Beit Shammai [who represent the attribute of strict Judgment, where outer pretexts like scorching a dish or finding a more beautiful woman might seem to have standing].

column11: Eruvin 13b: ‘The Sages taught the following baraita: For two and a half years, Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel disagreed. These say: It would have been preferable had man not been created than to have been created. And those said: It is preferable for man to have been created than had he not been created. Ultimately, they were counted and concluded: It would have been preferable had man not been created than to have been created. However, now that he has been created, he should examine his actions that he has performed and seek to correct them.
